We write $\|\cdot\|$ for the Euclidean norm and $I_{d}$ for the
$d\times d$ identity matrix.
For symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$, the notation $A\preceq B$
means that $B-A$ is positive semidefinite.

Let
$O(n):=\{O\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:O^{\top}O=I_{n}\}$
denote the real orthogonal group, equipped with Haar probability
measure.
It has two components, $\{\det O=+1\}$,
$\{\det O=-1\}$, and each have Haar probability $1/2$.
For $b\in\{-1,+1\}$, we write $\mu_{n,b}$ for Haar probability
measure conditioned on $\det O=b$.

We restrict the target class to centered Gaussians.
This restriction removes the hardness of locating the target and isolates the difficulty of sampling with an unknown covariance.
For an integer $d\geq 1$ and a parameter $\kappa\geq 1$, without loss of generality, we normalize the spectral bounds to $1$
and $\kappa$ by rescaling and consider
the precision class
$\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}:=\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}:A=A^{\top},\quad I_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}\right\}.$

An input $A\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}$ specifies the quadratic
potential $f_{A}(x):=\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax$ and the target distribution
$\pi_{A}:=N(0,A^{-1})$.
At a point $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, the exact first-order oracle returns

$\operatorname{FO}_{A}(x):=\bigl(f_{A}(x),\nabla f_{A}(x)\bigr)=\left(\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax,Ax\right).$
(1)

On this class, exact first-order access is equivalent to exact
matrix–vector access.
Indeed, a first-order response contains $Ax$, while a
matrix–vector response determines both the gradient $Ax$
and the function value $\frac{1}{2}\langle x,Ax\rangle$.
Thus the exact value-and-gradient, gradient-only, and
matrix–vector query complexities coincide.

A randomized algorithm chooses its queries and stopping decisions
as Borel functions of its internal randomness and previous oracle
responses, where the randomness is independent of the input.
Its output may be any $\mathbb{R}^{d}$-valued Borel function of
the same information.
The algorithm has fixed query budget $T$ if it makes
at most $T$ queries for every admissible input and every
realization of its internal randomness.

For probability measures $P$ and $Q$ on a common measurable space,
their total variation distance is
$\operatorname{TV}(P,Q):=\sup_{B}|P(B)-Q(B)|=\frac{1}{2}\int|p-q|\,d\lambda,$

where the supremum ranges over measurable sets, and $p$ and $q$
are the densities of $P$ and $Q$ with respect to any common
dominating measure $\lambda$.
In particular,
$|\mathbb{E}_{P}h-\mathbb{E}_{Q}h|\leq\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)$
for every measurable function $h$ taking values in $[0,1]$.

For a fixed input $A$, let $\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}$ denote
the law of the algorithm’s output, with all internal
randomness included.
For $0<\varepsilon<1$, define

$Q_{G}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon):=\inf\left\{T\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}:\begin{array}[]{l}\exists\,\mathrm{Alg}\text{ with fixed query budget }T\\[2.0pt]
\text{such that }\displaystyle\sup_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}}\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}},\pi_{A}\bigr)\leq\varepsilon\end{array}\right\}.$
(2)

The accuracy requirement is uniform over inputs and concerns
the output law after averaging over the algorithm’s seed.
Throughout the paper, query budgets are deterministic caps
on the number of queries in each run, rather than bounds
on the expected number of queries.

We use a construction similar to that in [22, Section 9.2],
with a cosine eigenvalue grid (Chebyshev nodes) and a random orthogonal rotation, while extending the spectral
interval from $[1,2]$ to $[1,\kappa]$.
For $d\geq 2$ and $\kappa\geq 2$, define

$\theta_{i}=\frac{(i-\tfrac{1}{2})\pi}{d},\qquad\lambda_{i}=\frac{\kappa+1}{2}+\frac{\kappa-1}{2}\cos\theta_{i},\qquad\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}).$
(11)

Draw $O\sim\operatorname{Haar}(\mathrm{O}(d))$, independently
of the algorithm’s private randomness, and set $A=O\Lambda O^{\top}$.
The associated potential and target are
$f_{A}(x)=x^{\top}Ax/2$ and $\pi_{A}=N(0,A^{-1})$.

The spectrum is deterministic and may be supplied to the algorithm.
In particular, the Gaussian normalizing constant is known.
The unknown component is the random eigenbasis represented by $O$.

Remark 4.2 (Comparison with $\kappa=2$ case).
At $\kappa=2$, the spectrum in
Eq. (11) recovers the original construction in [22].
More generally, if $A_{2}$ denotes the original precision matrix
with the same rotation $O$, then
$A=(\kappa-1)A_{2}-(\kappa-2)I_{d}$.
Thus one matrix–vector reply for either matrix determines
the corresponding reply for the other.
The proof compares $\sum_{i}\cos(n\theta_{i})\langle x,Oe_{i}\rangle^{2}$ with $\|x\|^{2}$, where $n=2q+1$.
For the output of a $q$-query algorithm, the ratio is at most $d^{-\Omega(1)}$ in absolute value
(Lemma 4.4), whereas under the target the ratio of the means has absolute value
$e^{-\Theta(n/\sqrt{\kappa})}$ (Lemma 4.5).
Hence the test works for $n$ up to order $\sqrt{\kappa}\log d$, rather than $\log d$ as at
$\kappa=2$, which is the source of the factor $\sqrt{\kappa}$ in
Theorem 4.1.

Lemma 4.6 (Admissibility).
For every $O\in\mathrm{O}(d)$, the matrix $A=O\Lambda O^{\top}$
satisfies $I_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}$.

Since $0<\theta_{i}<\pi$, we have $-1<\cos\theta_{i}<1$,
and hence $1<\lambda_{i}<\kappa$.
As $A=O\Lambda O^{\top}$ with $O$ orthogonal, this gives
$I_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}$.

The potential $V_{A}(x)=\tfrac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax$ is $C^{\infty}$
with Hessian $\nabla^{2}V_{A}(x)=A$.
Thus it is $1$-strongly convex and $\kappa$-smooth.
Moreover, $V_{A}(0)=0$ and
$V_{A}(x)\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\|x\|^{2}>0$ for $x\neq 0$,
so $0$ is its unique minimizer.

Theorem 4.1 (Extension to general $\kappa$).
For every fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$, there exists $d_{0}(\delta)$ such
that, for every integer $d\geq d_{0}(\delta)$,
$2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}$, and $0<\varepsilon\leq 1/10$,
$Q_{G}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon)\geq\frac{\delta}{256}\sqrt{\kappa}\log d.$
